newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian commodities seen gaining from rupiah.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian commodities seen gaining from rupiah.

text.p: The weakening of Indonesia's currency against the U.S. dollar will boost the competitiveness of the country's agricultural exports but could burden importers, analysts and industry sources said on Wednesday.
"There will be a windfall for some sectors in the short term," H.S. Dillion, vice-president of the Asian Society of Agricultural Economists, told Reuters.
"But this would benefit mostly traders and speculators. The farmers will not gain from the (currency) turbulence as supply in most commodities is fixed."

Indonesia is among the world's top producers of palm oil, coffee, cocoa, rubber, tin and tea. The archipelago, with a population of more than 200 million people, is also a major importer of items such as wheat, corn and soybeans.
Palm olein or cooking oil prices jumped after speculative offshore attacks on the Indonesian rupiah plunged the currency to a historic low against the U.S. dollar on Monday.
The rupiah fell to 2,665 against the dollar and although it had regained some strength since, it still remained volatile. The rupiah was quoted at 2,570 in early afternoon trade.
At the height of the speculative attacks, the rupiah had shed over nine percent against the dollar from a week ago.

"The decline should spur exports of palm olein because we will become more competitive," one trader said. "Local prices increased because they had to adjust to export prices which are quoted in U.S. dollars."
Palm olein prices have increased by more than four percent from last Friday to 1,430-40 rupiah (52 cents) a kg in Jakarta.

"I see palm olein exports increasing in the near term because of the decline," one trader said. "Prices in Europe are still at a premium to local prices, and we can be more competitive, although we will face competition from Malaysia."
Cocoa and coffee traders also said the rupiah's decline would boost competitiveness, but added that steady falls in international prices and tight supply posed limitations.
"It will give a competitive edge for fresh deals," one cocoa trader said. "One company is sitting pretty because it has a large amount of stocks and is selling to the United States."
Another trader said the decline should give the market a bullish trend, but added that cocoa arrivals in the key growing region of South Sulawesi had been slow due to weather woes.
A coffee trader in the South Sumatra's Lampung growing region said players with long-term contracts would benefit, but added that tight supply kept fresh business to a minimum.

"It has been acknowledged that the Indonesian coffee crop this year would be lower by about 30 percent or more," he said. "Prices in London have been declining, and so the benefits are going to be very limited at the moment."
"Players whose coffee is sitting at warehouses awaiting price-fixing can gain," he added.

Industry sources said Indonesian tin producers were expected to export more to take advantage of the rupiah's decline. Active Southeast Asian selling saw tin prices fall to a fresh 2-1/2 year low on Tuesday.
Indonesia's state-controlled PT Tambang Timah rose 100 rupiah (three cents) to 3,275 rupiah ($1.27) before easing to 3,200 rupiah ($1.25) on Wednesday.

For importers of items such as corn and soybeans, it was a time to hold back purchases. "Imports would naturally be more expensive and prices of the imports could be uncompetitive," one trader said. "We have to wait for the rupiah to stabilise."
